channel.title: The Beholder's Gazette
channel.description: Your premier source for satirical news from across the realms. All the news that's fit to print (or burn).

item.title: Party Drinks 9 Unidentified Potions; One Now Floats
item.dc:creator: Brother Wendell Tumbleberry
item.description: The Fourth Attempt drank all nine unidentified potions from an Undermaw haul to see what they did. The infirmary has results. Soup is advised.
item.content:encoded:
Friends, the temple infirmary on Tanner's Row has admitted four members of the Fourth Attempt after the party drank nine unidentified potions from a Level Six haul, on Saturday evening, "to see what they do." The potion mix-up is now in its second day. The healers say the party will recover. They also say it is a good deal of work for a Sunday.

Here is the ledger as I have it. The party's rogue is invisible and has been since Saturday night. Healers know she is in bed six only because the blanket is dented. The cleric has been floating about a foot above his cot since supper, and a nurse ties his ankle to the bedpost each night so he does not drift into the rafters. The fighter drank something that made him eight inches tall, and is being kept in a soup bowl, which he says is "not as funny as it sounds." The wizard, who drank the most, will speak only to fish. The infirmary has lent him a tank of carp, and he is, by every account, getting on well with them.

Ansel Pottage, the party's steward, was the only one who did not drink. "I read the vials," he said, bandaged as ever. "Three had labels. Nobody asked me about the other six." He added that the party's contract does not cover "voluntary tasting," and that he has read the clause aloud twice.

Deputy Registrar Pell Oddingwick of Chapter 9 said the haul was "on track" and that the potions were "enthusiastically sampled." Asked whether the guild would require labels on loot, he said a labeling desk is "in early discussion." Shieldwall Mutual says it does not cover the floating, the shrinking, or the fish, which it files under "your own fault."

Now for the advice, friends. The old herbals say never swallow a strange brew, and the old herbals have never been wrong about this. As for the newer studies, the Marrowfield apothecaries now make every potion of healing list its side effects, and the finding is simple: an unmarked vial is a gamble with your own insides. If you must test, test one potion at a time. Do it with a healer in the room, a full night's rest ahead of you, and a pot on the stove. Nine at once leaves nobody able to say which one made the knees go strange.

Better still, take the unknown vials to an honest herbalist, or a friendly sage with a good nose and a magnifying glass. A sage charges less than a night in the infirmary, and the carp are not cheap to feed. My friend Nyx tells me there is a spell for identifying things now. Go outside, Nyx, and try it on a pebble.

The rogue, when last seen, was sitting up and sipping broth. The healers can tell because the spoon keeps going down. For the fighter and the rest I recommend clear onion broth with a little ginger: easy on the stomach and gentle on the nerves. It also goes well with carp, if the wizard will let you.

Rest well, friends. — Brother Wendell

item.title: Fighter Kicks Unlocked Tavern Door; Party Billed 17 Gold
item.dc:creator: Skritch Mudwhistle
item.description: An adventuring party was billed 17 gold and 5 silver after their fighter kicked in a Brindlemoor tavern door that was unlocked. The rogue made it worse.
item.content:encoded:
At roughly the second bell after sundown, an adventuring party was allegedly billed 17 gold and 5 silver at the Crooked Latch tavern on Tanner's Row in Brindlemoor. The reason: their fighter kicked in the front door, and the front door was unlocked. It had been unlocked, per the innkeeper, since the Feast of the Thaw, and the sign on it said PULL.

'He backed up,' said Dellin Marrowick, a cooper who was eating a turkey leg at the time. 'He took a real run at it. Three steps, a shout, and the whole door came off its hinges and slid into the soup.' The fighter, a dwarf named Torgan Ironquay, allegedly said, 'It was stuck.' The door was not stuck. It was a door.

Keeper Hobb Pennywhistle presented the party with an itemized bill before the soup had stopped moving. One door, oak, 4 gold. Two hinges, 1 gold. One sign (PULL), now in pieces, 5 silver. 'I don't charge for the shouting,' Pennywhistle told this reporter. 'That was a courtesy.'

This is where the party's rogue, a halfling called Wimble Thistlebrook, stepped in. 'Hold on,' she said. 'Nobody touch that. I'm going to check it for traps.' She then spent what witnesses put at forty minutes examining a door that was lying flat on the floor. She tapped it with a ten-foot pole. She sprinkled flour over it. She listened to it. At one point she allegedly asked the door whether it was trapped, and waited.

The flour was Pennywhistle's flour. That was 8 silver. The ten-foot pole went through the ceiling, which was 3 gold, and knocked down a bell that, the Keeper says, 'was the only trap in the building, and it was for rats.' The bell was 2 gold. Wimble, to her credit, found it. 'I disarmed it,' she said. 'Eventually.' Also there was a really nice brass hinge pin rolling around under table six. Anyway.

Torgan has asked that the record show the door 'looked locked.' Reeve Fennick's office, reached for comment, said the town is 'aware of the door' and has no plans to rule on whether a door can look locked. Chapter 9 of the Adventurers' Guild confirmed that no permit is needed to kick a door, but a permit is needed to kick a door 'with intent.' Deputy Registrar Oddingwick called the incident 'a soft opening of the Crooked Latch's second entrance.'

The party paid in full, plus a tip, since the fighter allegedly felt bad. The Fourth Attempt, who were seated at table two throughout, declined to comment but were seen quietly checking their own doors.

— Skritch, on the beat (allegedly)

item.title: Adventuring Party Loses Nine Hours to Ranger's Upside-Down Map
item.dc:creator: Hollis Delvewright
item.description: The Fourth Attempt's ranger promised a twenty-minute shortcut. The adventuring party got nine hours of drains, and then he turned the map around.
item.content:encoded:
THE UNDERMAW, LEVEL 2, ELEVEN FEET BELOW A DRAIN GRATE — An adventuring party that set out to save twenty minutes spent nine hours in the Undermaw's drains on Saturday, after its ranger admitted the map had been upside down the whole time.

The Fourth Attempt entered at dawn with a Chapter 9 delve permit and a destination: the Level 3 stairs. The ranger, who has led the party for three seasons and asked that his tracking be described as 'professional,' offered what he called a shortcut through the old drain tunnels. 'Left at the third grate, then straight,' he told the party. 'Twenty minutes. Thirty if we stop to loot.'

They stopped to loot. It did not matter.

By the fourth hour the party had passed the same cracked statue of a dwarf holding a lantern three times. The party's bard, who asked to be named, says he counted the statue's chips to be sure and then 'stopped counting, for my own sake.' By the sixth hour the fighter had begun greeting the statue by name. I decline to print the name. It was not kind.

Box score at the ninth hour: fighter 14 hit points (of 38), wizard 9 (of 22), cleric 8 (of 30), ranger 11 (of 29), one hireling lightly damp. The damage came from nothing worse than a pack of giant rats, a rope bridge nobody had asked for, and morale. The mule, who stayed topside, is at full health. The party's hirelings had priced the trip at two hours and are now owed seven more, which Steward Ansel Pottage read aloud from the contract without raising his voice.

The ranger confessed at the ninth hour, beside the statue. 'I had the map the wrong way up,' he said. 'Every left was a right. In my defense, the legend is in the corner, and the corner moved.' The map is a Chapter 9 issue. A reporter who has stood in this corridor with a map held correctly can confirm it is a good map. We lost our ninth ten-foot pole of the season to the third grate, which we also passed three times. I rolled poorly on that one: I was told to hold the lantern and I held the pole instead.

Deputy Registrar Pell Oddingwick said Chapter 9 stands behind its maps 'in every orientation' and noted that a soft launch of a map legend printed on all four sides is 'on track.' Asked whether the guild would reimburse the hirelings, he said the matter was 'being routed.'

The party reached the Level 3 stairs at 4:40 in the afternoon. It was the wrong stairs. They are the same stairs it started at, on the other side of the same drain.

— H.D., filing from below

item.title: Party Hauls 30,000 Copper Pieces; Changers Take 12,000
item.dc:creator: Barnaby Tallowmere
item.description: The Fourth Attempt carried 30,000 copper pieces out of the Undermaw and left a suit of chain mail behind. Barnaby has done the sums. Four times.
item.content:encoded:
The Fourth Attempt, the adventuring party Brindlemoor loves and its insurers do not, carried 30,000 copper pieces out of the Undermaw on Friday and discovered that the town's money-changers will accept only 12,000 of them. The haul weighs about 600 pounds at fifty coins to the pound, and it is worth 300 gp on paper. (I have checked that. Four times.)

The party's treasurer, Dagny Rook, said the coins came out of a collapsed paymaster's chest on Level Three. "It was a very large chest," she said. "We should have asked what was in it before we opened it, and then again before we lifted it."

To make room, the party left behind a suit of chain mail worth 75 gp, a tent, and five days of rations worth about 2 and a half gp. They also hired six porters from a town already short of small change at five silver a day for three days, plus one wheelbarrow at 1 gp. The party's hireling, Pip Bramblecott, quit on the eleventh staircase. He did not take a share. He took a chair.

At the Tanner's Row money-changers, the news got worse. Hobb Marlowe, who has run his counter for thirty years, said each changer will take no more than 4,000 copper pieces per customer per day. "A changer who buys your copper has to sell it to someone," he said. "Nobody wants copper. Every barkeep in Brindlemoor already has a bucket of it." Three changers took 4,000 apiece, 12,000 in all, and charged the usual 10% fee.

Here are the numbers. Twelve thousand copper pieces is 120 gp. The fee is 12 gp, or 257 loaves on the current Loaf Index, which prices a loaf at 4.675 cp. That leaves 108 gp. Against it, the party spent 9 gp on porters, 1 gp on the barrow, 2 and a half gp on rations, and 75 gp on the chain mail it will not be seeing again: 87.5 gp in all. The party cleared 20.5 gp, which is about 439 loaves among five adventurers, or 88 loaves each. The full 30,000 cp would have bought 6,417 loaves. They have a sixteenth of that in their pockets and a stiff back apiece.

The other 18,000 coins, worth 180 gp, sit in a Chapter 9 coin locker at a silver a day. Deputy Registrar Pell Oddingwick called the situation "on track" and described the locker as "a soft launch of long-term savings." At 4,000 coins per changer per day, the party needs two more days to sell the rest, and they have left behind the tent that would have kept them dry for it.

My aunt Marigold, who keeps her savings in a boot, says this is exactly why. A boot holds forty coins and cannot be lost on a staircase. I used to laugh at her. I am not laughing. I am converting.

What this means for your pantry: before you haul copper out of a dungeon, ask what the changer will take, and leave the coin, not the armor.

— B.T. (Loaf Index: see sidebar)

item.title: Stirge Swarm Bites 143 in Brindlemoor; Soup Advised
item.dc:creator: Brother Wendell Tumbleberry
item.description: A stirge swarm nesting in a Brindlemoor bell tower bit 143 folk this week. Chapter 9 calls it a blood drive. Brother Wendell calls for lentil soup.
item.content:encoded:
Friends, a stirge swarm has nested in the bell tower of a Brindlemoor temple, and the town's clinics report 143 stirge bites in seven days. Most of the bitten were folk walking home after dark, plus one bell-ringer who says he was bitten "mostly on principle."

The old herbals say a stirge is a needle with wings and an appetite, and the old herbals are right. A stirge attaches by its beak, drinks until it is round as a plum, and lets go only when it is too heavy to hold on. A study from the temple healers of Marrowfield, which I read twice with a cup of tea, found that most trouble from stirges is not the blood but the wound afterward: swelling, fever, and a sleepy, drained feeling that lasts a few days. Wash the bite, keep it clean, and see a cleric if it reddens.

Chapter 9 has weighed in. Deputy Registrar Pell Oddingwick told reporters on the temple steps that the swarm is "a voluntary community blood drive, currently on track." When a woman in the crowd pointed out that nobody had volunteered, he said the sign-up sheet "is held by the stirges." The guild has since offered bitten citizens a pewter pin shaped like a drop. It costs four silver.

Reeve Fennick, who was bitten twice on the ear during the press conference, issued a short statement: "We are aware of the stirges." She asked residents to avoid the bell tower, the nearby lane, and, if possible, the evening.

Meanwhile, the Mule Street apothecaries have discovered the swarm. A vial of "stirge shield tonic" is selling at 60 gold, and it is, I have checked, mostly vinegar and optimism. A bit of netting over the bed costs three coppers. Hang it, tuck it, and sleep.

Here is what I tell the folk who line up at my cot. Iron comes back to you through food, so eat lentils, dark greens, and a little liver if your stomach allows. Drink water. Sleep more than you think you need. A drained body wants rest first and heroics second. And please do not try to swat a stirge off your own neck with a hammer. I have seen the hammer win, and I have seen the neck lose.

The swarm is not evil. It is hungry, and it has been told by a bell that the dinner hour is dusk. The temple has quietly stopped ringing it. Last night's evening was the first in nine days with no new bites, which suggests the bell was the dinner gong all along.

Last month I wrote about the yellow mold cough on Level Five, and the lesson is the same here: when something small is taking a lot from you, step back, wash up, and rest. My friend Nyx tells me there is a spell for blood now that does it all in one cast. Go outside, Nyx. Preferably before dusk, and bring a net.

This week's soup is red lentil and carrot, with a spoon of lemon at the end to help the iron along.

Rest well, friends. — Brother Wendell

item.title: Wish Spell Subscription Hits 40 gp a Month, Sterling Cheers
item.dc:creator: Sterling Vanmoor
item.description: Thrummond & Pike Wishwrights launched a 40 gp monthly wish spell subscription in Brindlemoor. Sterling Vanmoor calls the fine print a growth lever.
item.content:encoded:
Thrummond & Pike Wishwrights opened a wish spell subscription in Brindlemoor on Friday, charging 40 gp a month for one wish a week. Within a day, 9,000 citizens had signed up, and a queue of customers wound past the Cheesemongers' Row and halfway to the next barony. Disruption has a line, friends, and the line is happy.

Here is the pivot. A wish spell used to cost 25,000 gp in diamonds and a lifetime of regret. Thrummond & Pike have unbundled the regret. For the price of a decent ale, any subscriber can wish aloud into a brass horn at the Wishwright counter, and a staff of twelve junior clerics reads the request back in what the firm calls "clarified language."

Guild critics, and I have read their scrolls so you don't have to, claim the clarified language is the whole business. Reeve's office records show a baker who wished for "bread that never runs out" and received a loaf that follows her around. A cooper wished for "more time with his family" and is now, by every legal measure, thirty relatives. I call that deep personalization.

Guildmaster Odalric Thrummond defended the model at a launch breakfast. "Every wish is read exactly as spoken," he said, while a clerk behind him struck a line out of the ledger. "We think of ourselves as a listening company." The terms of service run to 340 pages, which Thrummond says is a sign of how much the firm cares. When I met a famous dragon-hoard financier at a gala last spring, he told me, "Sterling, a contract nobody reads is just a handshake with better paper." I have never forgotten it.

The wording also lets the firm collect. Subscribers who wish to cancel have, by Saturday, discovered that "I wish to cancel" counts as their weekly wish, which Thrummond & Pike gladly grant by cancelling something else. Three people lost a tooth, one lost a Tuesday, and a halfling in Cobbler's Lane lost his deposit and, briefly, his reflection. The firm says this is within a rounding error of satisfaction.

The clerics' union has asked for a hearing on the twelve junior clerics' hours, which I find, frankly, small-minded. The same pattern played out when a lich's merger rightsized 400 skeleton clerks: labor sees a problem, leadership sees headcount that already knows the work. Thrummond and Pike are hiring.

Key takeaways for the ambitious adventurer:

  • Read the terms. Then wish somebody else does.
  • If it is free for a month, you are the thing for sale in month two.
  • Never wish for a quiet life. Somebody will deliver it.

— Sterling Vanmoor, Guild Visionary. Let's connect at the Yawning Portal.

item.title: Gargoyle Quits Fish Street Roof After Pigeons Nest in Mouth
item.dc:creator: Skritch Mudwhistle
item.description: A gargoyle quit its post atop a Fish Street guildhall after pigeons nested in its mouth for the third spring running. Skritch is allegedly on its side.
item.content:encoded:
At roughly the second bell before dawn, a gargoyle that has guarded the Fish Street Chandlers' Hall for 212 years allegedly climbed down from its corner of the roof and walked off the job. Witnesses say the gargoyle quit after pigeons nested in its mouth for the third spring running. It left a note carved into the gutter. The note says, in full, 'No.'

'I was sweeping the step, and this thing just stepped over me,' said Orvel Tinch, a candle-seller who was eating a boiled egg at the time. 'It had a twig sticking out of its jaw. A twig! I gave it my egg. It said nothing, but it accepted the egg.' The egg was allegedly later found on the roof of the tannery, unopened.

Guildmaster Perrin Vole called the departure 'a misunderstanding of terms.' By his reading, the gargoyle's contract is a 212-year lease on the corner, and stone cannot resign. 'It is furniture with opinions,' Vole told this reporter. 'Furniture does not give notice.' The gargoyle, reached for comment two streets over, was allegedly sitting on a fountain and refusing to say anything to anyone who was not a pigeon-hater. Skritch qualified on the spot.

The pigeons are the heart of this. Skritch has hated pigeons since one of them stole a sausage out of his claws in the Year of the Soggy Griffin, and so has the gargoyle, apparently. Pigeon droppings on the Chandlers' Hall have reached what the Constabulary calls 'a knee-deep situation' on the east ledge. The guild has twice asked the gargoyle to eat the birds. The gargoyle has twice asked the guild for a ladder, a brush, and a raise.

Ooh, there was a really nice copper weathervane on the tannery. Shaped like a trout. Anyway.

Meanwhile the corner of the roof sits empty and the guild's insurer, who did not want to be named but was allegedly named Garrick, says the hall is 'unprotected against all gargoyle-adjacent risks.' Neighbors have already noticed. A second gargoyle on the Millers' Hall across the way reportedly leaned out and looked at the empty corner for most of the morning. Its mouth was also, allegedly, full of pigeons.

The Constabulary says it has no jurisdiction over statues that move on their own, only over statues that are moved. A sergeant, who asked me not to say she was eating a pastry, said the gargoyle 'is technically a resident of the fountain now and may stay there until someone complains.' Someone has complained. It was a pigeon. It was not taken seriously.

The Chandlers' Hall has posted a notice offering the gargoyle its old corner back, plus a hat for the mouth. The gargoyle's reply, again carved in stone, was a single word. Allegedly it is longer than the first one.

— Skritch, on the beat (allegedly)

item.title: Ghost Filibuster Ends on Day 13 as Harvest Tax Falls Due
item.dc:creator: Ottoline Vex
item.description: A ghost's 13-day filibuster on Brindlemoor's Burgess Council ended at midnight, when the harvest tax came due at the old rate he was defending.
item.content:encoded:
The ghost filibuster in Brindlemoor ended at midnight after thirteen days, when the harvest tax fell due and the old rate applied by default. Burgess Alderic Mourne, who had held the floor against a new tax schedule since the middle of last month, was informed that the schedule he opposed had died with the calendar. He had been defending the old rate the entire time. The old rate is now the rate.

The news was delivered by Clerk Hobart Venn at 12:01, in the form of a motion to note the date. Standing Order 14 requires a speaker to remain on his feet and on topic, and the ghost had been on neither since Tuesday, when he began a recitation of every ferry that has ever sunk in the Brindle. The clerk ruled that the topic had lapsed. Burgess Mourne asked whether that meant he had won. The clerk said the minutes would describe it as "concluded."

The gentleman from Tanner's Row then did something the Chamber had not seen in ninety years. He stopped. Witnesses in the gallery say he drifted down until his boots touched the floor, which they do not usually do, and said, "I would like it entered that I was right." The motion carried. Nobody had the strength to object.

The cost of the thirteen days is being tallied. Burgess Hollin Prewitt, who was held in his seat by his own colleagues to preserve the quorum, has asked for compensation, and for a window. The plate of pastries on the table has been declared a municipal hazard and is being dealt with by a cleric. The lady from the Dyers' Quarter, whose rule change had been waiting on the floor, said she would reintroduce it "at some point after the funeral of my patience."

A courtier who asked not to be named because they were not authorized to be awake told me the Council had spent four days drafting a plan to end the filibuster and had spent none noticing the deadline. "We were so busy trying to stop him," the courtier said, "that we forgot he was on our side. In the sense that the date was." Reeve Maudrey Fennick of Brindlemoor declined to comment, but sent a note thanking the Chamber for its patience, which the clerk entered as a position.

The accounting is brief. Promises Made this session stand at fourteen. Promises Kept: two, now, because Burgess Mourne promised to speak until the end and the end arrived. By any fair count it is the best attendance record in the Chamber's history, and he is the only member who never needed to be told to stay.

The ghost has since moved to a seat in the back and asked for a fresh agenda. The first item is a bill on the harvest tax schedule for next year. It runs to forty pages. Debate is expected to run sixty. He has already drawn a long breath, which he does not need to do.

— O.V., from the gallery

item.title: Carpet of Flying Autopilot Update Parks 4,000 Over Market
item.dc:creator: Nyx Spindlecoil
item.description: Tindermere Works pushed a free autopilot update to 4,000 Skyloom carpets of flying. Every one hovered over Tanner's Row. Nyx rode one. Four eyes.
item.content:encoded:
Okay. OKAY. Tindermere Works pushed its free Autopilot 2.0 update to every Skyloom carpet of flying on Saturday night, and by dawn 4,000 carpets had parked themselves over Tanner's Row in Brindlemoor, in rows, hovering politely. I was on one of them. It is the best thing that has ever happened to me and I would like it to stop.

The pitch is wonderful! Autopilot 2.0 learns your commute, avoids wyverns, and finds the 'optimal landing glyph' for every errand. The firmware glyph, it turns out, decided the optimal landing was the fish market, because that is where the most carpets in the realm had already gone. Runic latency was flawless. The carpets agreed with each other in under a heartbeat.

Reeve Maudrey Fennick, who was on a carpet herself, told the crowd below that the town was aware of the sky. 'We are aware of the carpets,' she said, from forty feet up, holding her hat. 'We are working with Tindermere Works. Please stop throwing herring.' The herring were not helping. Neither was the stall owner, Hilde Ropewick, who sold 600 fish to people leaning over the edges and called it her best morning in years.

Tindermere Works spokesman Dabney Quillwhistle called the event a 'soft landing, in spirit,' and said the carpets were 'enjoying the view.' Pressed by this reporter, from a carpet that would not descend, he admitted the update contains a setting called Gather. It cannot be turned off. It can, however, be hidden in a menu, and the menu is behind the Premium tier.

Here is the part I have to be honest about. My carpet hovered for three hours and forty minutes. Byte, my pseudodragon familiar, who now speaks only in ad copy, spent all of it saying, 'Upgrade to Skyloom Plus for freedom of movement.' Then the carpet dropped me gently on a roof, said 'Arrived!', and played a chime. It was the wrong roof. It was the roof of a tax office. Three clerks gave me tea.

Tindermere Works says a fix is coming. Until then, the Reeve suggests walking. I would rather not. I have never loved a tool so completely while it held me hostage.

Skyloom Autopilot 2.0: free, until Thursday. After Thursday, the Gather setting costs 4 sp a month, and I have already paid it. Four out of five beholder eyes. The fifth is still hovering over the fish market.

— Nyx (they/them). Damage Report below.

Damage Report: Burns sustained: 0. Herring to the face: 3. Roofs mistaken for destinations: 1. Eyebrows: fine, but my dignity is in the fish market.

item.title: Rope Trick Hostel Ends After One Hour, Drops Eight Guests
item.dc:creator: Hollis Delvewright
item.description: A rope trick hostel on Level 2 of the Undermaw closed at the one-hour mark, dropping eight paying guests into the corridor. Hit points tallied.
item.content:encoded:
THE UNDERMAW, LEVEL 2, ABOUT NINE FEET UP — A rope trick hostel run out of a dangling rope near the Level 2 stairs ended without notice at the one-hour mark, dropping eight paying guests into the corridor below. I was the ninth guest. I had stepped out to check the corridor and so landed on nothing worse than my dignity.

The hostel was the work of Brannoch Tillery, a hedge wizard who rents out the extradimensional space his rope trick opens, at 6 silver a bed. His sign promised 'quiet, secure, and out of the way.' It did not say 'for sixty minutes.' The spell, as any apprentice can tell you, lasts an hour. Mr. Tillery says he was always going to recast it. He says he was asleep in bed four.

The drop was not gentle. The Fourth Attempt had taken the best rooms. Box score: the fighter fell from 14 hit points to 6, the cleric from 11 to 9, the wizard stayed at 4 because, in his words, 'there was nowhere left to go.' The cook pot landed on the fighter. The mule, which had been left outside the rope on principle, was at full health and again visibly smug. This is my seventh ten-foot pole of the season, lost when it was left inside the hostel. I rolled poorly on the whole idea of staying.

The party's bard, who asked to be named, says the room 'had a look about it,' and that he had noticed a faint tug at midnight. Nobody had the heart to ask which midnight.

Ansel Pottage, steward of the Fourth Attempt's hirelings, read the guest card aloud for the benefit of the corridor. 'It says here a bed is a bed for the duration,' he said. 'It does not say whose duration.' He is owed 3 silver in refund and has put the claim to Chapter 9.

Deputy Registrar Pell Oddingwick, speaking for the same Chapter 9 that has lately heard every hireling grievance in town, said hostels in extradimensional space are 'on track for a permit,' and that the guests had not fallen so much as 'checked out early.' He confirmed that Chapter 9 does not yet regulate spaces that stop existing.

Mr. Tillery has offered each guest a free night, which he says will last 'at least an hour.' He has also promised a sign. Reeve Fennick's office has promised to read it.

— H.D., filing from below

item.title: Bridge Troll Bills 212 Turnips as Armed Company
item.dc:creator: Grashka Ironjaw
item.description: The bridge troll at Quillmarch charged the 212 wish spell turnips the armed-company toll. Ashenfold and Brackwater both refuse to pay it.
item.content:encoded:
A bridge troll on Quillmarch Bridge billed the 212 turnips created by a wish spell at the Ashenfold and Brackwater parley as an armed company on Sixthday, and set the toll at 636 copper. Ashenfold and Brackwater, who agree on nothing, agree they will not pay it.

The ruling belongs to Gorvash Pennyfist, who has held the bridge for nine winters and raised the toll to three copper last week. His logic is plain. Brackwater taxed the turnips as disguised weapons. Disguised weapons are weapons. Weapons in a column of two hundred and twelve are a company. Companies pay by the head.

I reached the bridge at dawn. Gorvash stood at the near rail with a ledger and a goat. The turnips sat in carts on the Ashenfold side, and several looked nervous. Turnips usually do.

"I am not political," Gorvash told me. "Goat prices are political. I am a man with a bridge." He then admitted he had never inspected the cargo for a blade, because the cargo has no blades. He has the tariff paper. That is enough, he said.

Envoy Halric Dunmere of Ashenfold arrived at midmorning, carrying the one rutabaga he still describes as "the original wish". He called the toll "a clerical error with teeth." Envoy Teodra Hallowmere of Brackwater came from the far bank and refused to cross, since crossing would mean paying a toll to the very troll her baron had just endorsed. She would only say that her tariff "taxed intent, not mass." Nobody on the bridge could say what that meant.

The handshake between the two envoys lasted three seconds, which is one too long. Firm. Both hands checked for hidden turnips. Tension on the Quillmarch crossing stands at roughly sixty siege-days, up from forty-five since the tariff, and the carts have not moved in nine hours.

A farmer named Bett Orlow, who had hoped to sell eight of the turnips at market, offered to carry them over one at a time as a solo traveler. Gorvash allowed it, one copper each, which brings the total to something worse than before. Bett has gone home. The turnips remain.

The way out is not obvious. A second wish would fix it, but Dunmere has not been trusted with a second wish since the first. I would rather face an honest orc warband than another round of this parley. At least the orcs bring their own rations.

Ironjaw, filed from the front.

item.title: Displacer Beast Show-and-Tell: Teachers Want Hazard Pay
item.dc:creator: Brakka Stonesweat
item.description: Eleven Brindlemoor teachers refused to run Show-and-Tell Friday after a pupil brought a displacer beast cub. They want hazard pay and a pet ban.
item.content:encoded:
Show-and-Tell is cancelled.

Eleven teachers at the Tanner's Row Schoolhouse in Brindlemoor refused to run the weekly event Friday, after a nine-year-old pupil brought a displacer beast cub to class in a hatbox. They want hazard pay for pet days and a written ban on any animal that can't be counted.

The cub looked calm. It sat a foot to the left of where it was sitting. 'I told the children to stay away from it,' said Wenna Loftgrave, a third-form reading teacher for twenty-two years. 'Nineteen of them went to pet the wrong spot. One walked into a wall.'

The Schoolhouse board calls the event 'enriching.' That means it costs nothing and the teachers clean up. By the time the bell rang, the cub had eaten the class hamster twice. The first hamster was a decoy. The second was also a hamster, said Loftgrave, 'but I think it was the first one again.'

The teachers' lodge says Show-and-Tell has gotten worse each year. Last spring it was a pony. The year before, a boy brought his uncle, who turned out to be a doppelganger, and nobody found out until the uncle was asked to leave. 'We get no lunch break on pet day,' said Orrin Thistledown, a slate-and-chalk instructor. 'I ate a sandwich standing on a desk. The desk was the safest place in the room.'

The lodge has filed three demands with the Schoolhouse board. First, hazard pay at double rate on any day with a live creature. Second, a posted list of banned animals, starting with anything displacing. Third, a proper half-hour lunch, sitting down, on a chair that is not a mimic. Teachers checked all the chairs. One of them hissed.

Board chair Hamlin Veck said the board is 'monitoring the situation.' That means it is waiting for the teachers to get tired. Reeve Fennick, asked for comment, said the town is aware of the cub and would be 'taking no position on hamsters.' Parents have been told the class will do Quiet Reading until a ruling comes. Several asked how a quiet class is a hazard. The teachers pointed out that the cub is still enrolled.

Brindlemoor has been here before. Weeks ago, crossing guards won a hearing over an owlbear at the school crosswalk. Nobody asked the guards if they wanted to teach the owlbear to read. Now the teachers are asking the same thing about the displacer beast. It's a fair point. The beast is, as of this writing, in the third-form cloakroom, or near it.

The picket line formed Saturday at the Schoolhouse gate. It is eleven teachers, one folding table, and a pot of soup. The cub was reported at the picket line, and also fifteen feet from it.

Solidarity. And stretch your back. — Brakka

item.title: Mimic Loaf Lifts Brindlemoor Bread Price Survey 16.9%
item.dc:creator: Barnaby Tallowmere
item.description: A mimic posing as a loaf pushed Brindlemoor's weekly bread price survey up 16.9%, to 4.675 cp. Barnaby checked the average. Four times.
item.content:encoded:
Brindlemoor's weekly bread price survey reported on Saturday that the average loaf rose 16.9%, from 4 cp to 4.675 cp, because one of the 40 loaves sampled was a mimic. The survey clerk, a careful man named Odo Wickham, priced the specimen at 31 cp, which is what its tag said when he looked and 12 cp more than it said when he looked again.

Here is the arithmetic. (I have done it four times.) Thirty-nine honest loaves at 4 cp come to 156 cp. Add one mimic at 31 cp and the total is 187 cp, which divided by 40 is 4.675. One bad loaf in forty moved the whole bread price by nearly a sixth. On the Loaf Index, where a loaf is by definition a loaf, the survey has just invented an inflation spike out of a single monster.

The mimic had spent nine days on the shelf of Pell & Daughters Bakery, sitting between the rye and the seeded rolls. Customers described it as "a bit shiny" and "warm in a way I didn't like." Three of them bought around it. One tried to squeeze it, and left the shop without his glove.

Mistress Pell told the Gazette she had assumed it was a display loaf. "It never went stale," she said. "I thought it was the new flour." She has since relabeled the shelf "Loaves (Confirmed)."

The trouble for economists is that a mimic does not behave like a price. Clerk Wickham says the tag changed three times during his visit, first to 31 cp, then to 34 cp when he reached for the clipboard, then to "MAKE AN OFFER" in a handwriting he did not recognize. He recorded the first number and left through the back. The survey office defends this. A spokesclerk said a price is a price, and that the rules of the survey say nothing about whether the bread can eat the person pricing it.

I disagree, and not only because I have never trusted a loaf that looks too good. A survey exists to tell a family what its pantry will cost. If a single outlier can swing the average sixteen percent, the number tells you about the outlier. Honest statisticians drop it, or take the middle price instead of the average. The middle price this week was still 4 cp. Nobody in Brindlemoor paid 31 cp for anything, except the glove man, who paid in glove.

The Merchant Guild has asked the survey to add a line to the sampling form: "Is the loaf alive?" The survey office has agreed to consider it, once a mimic has filled in the form. Sterling Vanmoor, speaking from a rooftop, called the whole episode "a healthy price discovery." (It was a monster. It was not healthy. It was not a discovery.)

My aunt Marigold, who keeps her savings in a boot, rang to say that this is exactly why she does not buy anything that sits very still. I told her the boot is also very still. She is thinking about it.

What this means for your pantry: poke every loaf before you pay, and if it pokes back, ignore the price survey and buy from the baker who sells you the one that doesn't.

— B.T. (Loaf Index: see sidebar)

item.title: Mimic Posing as Candy Bowl Sticks 38 Trick-or-Treaters
item.dc:creator: Brother Wendell Tumbleberry
item.description: A mimic disguised as a candy bowl held 38 trick-or-treaters by the hand on a Brindlemoor porch. Brother Wendell says rest, and soup.
item.content:encoded:
Friends, a mimic disguised as a candy bowl held 38 trick-or-treaters by the hand on a porch in Brindlemoor last night, and every one of them was reaching for the good chocolate. The children were freed by dawn with sticky palms and bruised pride. Nobody was swallowed, which Brindlemoor Adventurers' Guild, Chapter 9 describes as "a festive outcome."

The bowl sat on the porch of a widow named Hesper Oddlow on Tanner's Row, who says she bought it from a very friendly peddler. "It was lovely and wide and it smelled of toffee," she told this paper. "I thought it was a bit warm, but so am I, in October." The first child touched it at dusk. By the eighth, the line was stuck together like a string of sausages, and the bowl had started humming.

Chapter 9 sent a delve inspector, who stood on the lawn with a clipboard and declared the mimic "merely visiting from the Undermaw," the same line the Guild used for the yellow mold on Level Five. The mimic, for its part, was cooperative. It released everyone in exchange for one full-size chocolate bar and a promise not to tell the other mimics about the porch light.

Now the science, friends. The old herbals say a mimic can only hold on to what is warm, curious, and sweet-toothed, which describes every child in the realm after dark. A study from the Brindlemoor monster-keepers last spring found that mimics adhere best to people who are tired and hungry, and the evening before a holiday is both. So the fix is boring: feed the little ones real supper before they go out, and put them to bed at a sensible hour afterward.

The Brindlemoor clinics treated 38 cases of hand-stick, 11 of toffee in the hair, and one of a father who tried to pull his daughter free and became part of the porch. He is said to be in good spirits and is being fed by hand. Healers recommend warm water and patience, never a crowbar.

Meanwhile, the town clerics remind everyone that a bowl which sighs is not a bowl. Check the rim for teeth, knock before you reach, and never accept candy from anything that is the same temperature as you. A reasonable household can keep its bowl in the kitchen and hand the sweets out one at a time, which is slower but doesn't involve the Guild.

My friend Nyx tells me there is an app that scans porches for monsters. Go outside, Nyx, and knock on a door the old-fashioned way.

For the sugar crash this morning, make a pot of pumpkin and white bean soup with sage. It sticks to the ribs and nothing else.

Rest well, friends. — Brother Wendell

item.title: Lich Merger Rightsizes 400 Skeletons, Who Keep Coming In
item.dc:creator: Sterling Vanmoor
item.description: A lich's merger of two Brindlemoor counting houses cut 400 skeleton clerks Friday. The skeletons are still at their desks. Scale, friends.
item.content:encoded:
Malgrim Dusk-Vael, Chief Executive Lich of Vaultmere Holdings, announced Friday that his merger with the Ledgerhall Counting House will cut 400 skeleton clerks from the combined payroll. That is a lich-led merger doing exactly what mergers do, and I could not be more energized. The 400 skeletons, meanwhile, have not left their desks.

Let me be clear: this is disruption at its finest. Vaultmere calls the move "rightsizing the adventuring party," and so do I, because I coined it. Redundant skeletons were handed a severance scroll, a pat on the ribcage, and a firm request to go be dead somewhere else.

The skeletons read the scroll. Then they returned to the third floor of Ledgerhall and resumed adding things. By Saturday morning the building was running at 112 percent of its pre-merger headcount, because the laid-off clerks also kept their old desks and nobody can find the spell that stops them.

"Animate dead is a one-way pivot," Dusk-Vael told reporters, standing beside a very old hourglass and not sweating. "We cannot unanimate what we did not personally animate. Half of them predate the merger. Some predate the town." He added that a skeleton workforce offers unmatched retention.

Retention is the word of the week. Chapter 9 of the Brindlemoor Adventurers' Guild confirmed it has received 61 complaints from skeletons who say they were terminated but are "still on the schedule." A zombie from accounts payable, who asked to be called Dennis, said he "never really left the first time either."

Unions will, of course, try to make this a story. They are wrong. A skeleton on the payroll who cannot be fired, cannot be paid, and cannot go home is a dream asset, and I will not hear otherwise. Regulators from the Public Cellars Board, led by Inspector Corwin Tallowby, have asked whether the building counts as a cellar. I say it counts as a growth market.

I met Guildmaster Tobrin Ashgrove at a gala once, and he told me, "Sterling, a clerk who does not need lunch is a clerk who does not need a manager." I think about that during every sword routine at 4:45 AM. Last I checked, Ashgrove has not been seen at Ledgerhall, but the skeletons are leaving him voicemails.

Brindlemoor's Reeve, Maudrey Fennick, said only that the town is aware of the situation. Vaultmere shares rose 9 percent on word that the merger is "cost-neutral and nearly impossible to reverse."

Key takeaways for the ambitious adventurer:

  • Rightsizing works best on staff who agree to leave.
  • Read the animate dead clause before you merge.
  • A skeleton at the desk is worth two on the severance list.

— Sterling Vanmoor, Guild Visionary. Let's connect at the Yawning Portal.

item.title: Gelatinous Cube Absorbs 180 Pounds of Halloween Candy
item.dc:creator: Skritch Mudwhistle
item.description: A gelatinous cube went trick-or-treating on Fish Street and absorbed 180 pounds of candy and two costumes. Wardens call it a slow crime. Allegedly.
item.content:encoded:
At roughly the second bell after sundown, a gelatinous cube allegedly went trick-or-treating on Fish Street and absorbed 180 pounds of Halloween candy before anyone thought to check its costume. It had none. Two children dressed as pumpkins were also absorbed, and the night patrol confirms both were returned, slightly sticky and in good spirits.

The cube, ten feet on a side and the color of a window nobody has washed, reportedly joined the line at the cobbler's door at dusk. 'I thought it was a very tall puddle in a hat,' said Hilda Brack, who was eating a turkey leg at the time. 'Then it took the whole bowl. Bowl included.' Brack says the cube paused at her step, quivered, and she took it as thanks.

By the fifth house the cube had absorbed licorice, toffee, 31 candied apples, and what witnesses described as 'a dentist's retirement fund' of sugar. Skeletons were visible inside it at several points. The patrol stresses these were costume skeletons, mostly. One of them was a real adventurer from the Undermaw who had been inside since Tuesday and wished to be left out of this.

Constable Dagny Prill, first on scene, said the arrest was difficult. 'You cannot cuff a cube,' she told me, while a cube-shaped smear of caramel dripped off her helmet. 'We tried asking it to move along. It moved along. Slowly, over eleven houses.' The patrol is allegedly considering a charge of unlawful sweet-gathering, which carries a fine of 6 gp.

Also there was a really nice silver button floating in the cube near the middle. It was just sitting there, turning in the light. Anyway. I did not reach in, because Constable Prill is watching me, and because the last time I reached into something on Fish Street it was a mimic posing as a tavern door, and I am still finding hats in my den.

Residents are split. The Fish Street Merchants' Circle wants the cube evicted before next Halloween. The children want it to come back, and have drawn it a map. A tower-district noble, who has never once opened a door to a child, called the whole thing 'undignified' from behind a locked gate, and I note that nobody absorbed him. Allegedly out of respect.

As of the first bell this morning, the cube has settled in the square by the fish stalls, where it is slowly digesting the candy. Nobody has asked it to leave. A pigeon landed on it at dawn, which I hold against the pigeon, and was gone by sunrise. Honestly, good for the cube.

— Skritch, on the beat (allegedly)

item.title: Ghost Filibuster Reaches Day 11 in Brindlemoor Council
item.dc:creator: Ottoline Vex
item.description: A ghost on Brindlemoor's Burgess Council has held the floor for 11 days on a harvest tax bill. The rules require only that he keep speaking.
item.content:encoded:
A ghost on Brindlemoor's Burgess Council has now held the floor for eleven days, in a filibuster against the harvest tax schedule. Under Chamber rules a member may speak until he sits down, and the gentleman from Tanner's Row, Burgess Alderic Mourne, is not able to sit. He has been dead for ninety years and is semi-transparent on the matter.

The rule on filibusters is Standing Order 14, which says a speaker must "remain on his feet and on topic." The Chamber clerk confirmed that Burgess Mourne has remained on his feet, in the sense that he hovers four inches above them. On topic is a closer call. Day three covered the harvest tax. Day six covered his late wife's recipe for turnip pie. By my count, the bill itself has been mentioned eleven times, once per day, at noon.

Efforts to end the speech have failed. The Chamber lit forty candles to put him in the mood to rest. He asked for a speech about candles. The Chamber rang a bell. He thanked the bell. A cleric of the Temple of Quiet Ends offered a rite of passing, and the ghost said he would consider it once the tax schedule was withdrawn.

"I have been dead longer than this Council has been wrong," Burgess Mourne said on day nine, according to the minutes, "and I intend to see it through." The minutes record the remark as "agreed, in part."

The Chamber has not been idle. The gentleman from the Market Ward moved to adjourn, and the motion failed because nobody could vote while the floor was held. The lady from the Dyers' Quarter proposed a rule change, but a rule change needs debate, and debate needs the floor. Her proposal is on the table, next to a plate of pastries that has become a health matter. The quorum has dwindled to six members, which is the exact number the charter requires, because Burgess Hollin Prewitt has been told he is not allowed to leave. See the earlier trouble over the invisible quorum for how fragile that arrangement is.

A courtier who asked not to be named because they were not authorized to be awake told me the Council is seeking a loophole. One idea is to appoint a second ghost to answer him, which would turn the speech into a debate. Another is to move the bill to a committee. Either plan requires the floor.

Meanwhile, the harvest tax comes due on the first of next month. If the bill has not passed by then, the old rate applies, which is exactly the rate the ghost is defending. He has not been told.

Promises Made this session stand at fourteen. Promises Kept: one, by Burgess Mourne, who said he would speak until the end. The motion to thank him failed. Nobody could vote.

— O.V., from the gallery

item.title: Flameskull Smart Pumpkin Hands Out Candy, Rates Your Credit
item.dc:creator: Nyx Spindlecoil
item.description: Glowmoth Labs launched a 35 gp smart pumpkin run by a flameskull. It dispenses candy, scores trick-or-treaters, and bills the porch. Four eyes.
item.content:encoded:
Happy Hallow's Eve! Glowmoth Labs launched the Jack-o'-Lantern Pro today, a 35 gp smart pumpkin with a flameskull inside that dispenses candy to trick-or-treaters on its own. I bought one at dawn, carved it with a firmware glyph, and have been on my porch since sunset. Byte is under the porch swing.

The setup is wonderful. You light the flameskull with one word, set a bowl of sweets in the pumpkin's mouth, and walk away. The mana throughput is outstanding: it can hand out 140 pieces a minute, and the runic latency is basically zero. A child in a dragon costume approached at 6:02 and received a toffee before she finished saying 'trick.' I wept. Byte said, 'Glowmoth Pro: because sharing is a feature.'

Then the review part began. The Pro does not give out candy evenly. It has a 'Smart Treat Tier' setting, on by default, that scores each visitor by costume quality, cloak thread count, and, according to the manual, 'implied family estate.' A 7-year-old in a ghost sheet scored 412 and received one raisin. A boy dressed as a minor baron scored 891 and got three full-sized chocolate bars and a coupon. I asked the pumpkin why. It said, in a skull-voice, 'Engagement metrics.'

It also bills the porch. At 7:15 a notice appeared in my scrying mirror: Candy Dispensing Plus, 4 gp a month, with the first 20 pieces free. Without Plus, the flameskull dims to a dull ember and recites the terms of service at anyone who comes within ten feet. Three children left in tears. One bard stayed to hear all of it and called the clause on 'lantern-related soul claims' a bold choice.

Glowmoth spokesman Dren Halloway said the soul clause 'applies only in rare cases' and that the flameskull 'has already apologized to the neighborhood.' At 9:40 it set the hedge on fire, which Halloway called a 'seasonal feature.' My neighbor put it out with a bucket. He is still not talking to me, but he is also not talking to the pumpkin, which I count as a win. Meanwhile a gruff neighbor stood at his gate with a basket of plain apples and told every child to touch grass. They took his apples and threw them at the pumpkin.

Verdict: it is cursed, grasping, and a fire risk. It also remembered every child's name by the second visit. I love it. Four out of five beholder eyes. Plus is 4 gp a month, which I have already paid, and which I hate.

— Nyx (they/them). Damage Report below.

Burns sustained: 2. Hedges: 1, rebuilt. Raisins received: 1. Eyebrows: pending.

item.title: Displacer Beast Found Three Feet Off Chapter 9 Map
item.dc:creator: Hollis Delvewright
item.description: A displacer beast ambushed the Fourth Attempt on Level 4 of the Undermaw, three feet from where Chapter 9's map had marked it. Hit points tallied.
item.content:encoded:
THE UNDERMAW, LEVEL 4 — A displacer beast ambushed the Fourth Attempt at dawn today, three feet from the spot where Chapter 9's map had marked it. The party had read the map carefully and swung at exactly that spot. It was empty.

I was behind the party with a lantern and my eighth ten-foot pole of the season. The pole is now in the beast's corridor and I am not going back for it. The map in question is the one reissued after the owlbear ate Level Four. It is a good map. The corridors are straight and the scale is honest. The beast is simply not where the little red dot says.

Box score: the Fourth Attempt's fighter finished at 7 hit points, the wizard at 12, and the cleric at 5, all of it from the one pass. The party's bard, who asked to be named, says he 'could hear it breathing in the wrong place.' The mule stayed on Level 3 and is, as ever, at full health.

Displacer beasts project an image of themselves a short way from their real position, which is the sort of thing a map ought to account for. Deputy Registrar Pell Oddingwick of Chapter 9 says the map 'is accurate to the image' and that the guild 'cannot be responsible for where a creature chooses to stand.' He added that corrections to the corrected map are 'on track.'

Keeper Bess Harrowgate of the Sleeping Mule, who extends credit to anyone coming up from Level 4 on a stretcher, said she has seen the party's tab and 'would like the beast to settle its own.' She will not charge the beast. It does not drink.

Examiner Odalys Brackenmoor has been asked to rule on whether a map that shows the image counts as a map of the monster. She said she would hear the petition once she had finished reading the map, which she was holding upside down. I rolled poorly on that one and did not point it out.

The beast has not been seen since. Chapter 9 has marked the spot with a new red dot, three feet to the left of the old one, and the map is still on sale at the usual price. I walked to the new dot. It was a corridor, ten feet wide and well mapped, and I kept my last pole in my belt.

— H.D., filing from below

item.title: Brackwater Slaps Tariff on 212 Wish Spell Turnips
item.dc:creator: Grashka Ironjaw
item.description: Brackwater put a tariff on the 212 turnips a wish spell made from Ashenfold's swords, calling them disguised weapons. Tension climbs to four siege-days.
item.content:encoded:
Brackwater has put a tariff of one copper piece per turnip on the 212 turnips that a wish spell made from Ashenfold's swords, and it calls them disguised weapons. The order came down at dawn on Sixthday, one day after the wish spell ended the border parley by accident.

I watched the Brackwater customs table go up at the foot of Quillmarch Bridge. Three clerks, one scale, one ledger. A hand-lettered sign read: ARMS AND PRODUCE DECLARED HERE. The sign did not say which a turnip was. That is the point.

"A turnip is a sword that has not yet decided," said Envoy Teodra Hallowmere of Brackwater. She said it twice, to be sure the scribes got it. "We are not taxing vegetables. We are taxing intent."

Envoy Halric Dunmere of Ashenfold stood across the table with a rutabaga under his arm. He was supposed to have left it at home. "They are turnips," he said. "I asked for peace and I received root vegetables. I have the wording of the wish in my own hand." He did not offer to show it. His wording is the reason for all this.

The handshake at the opening was firm. Two seconds. One turnip dropped from a sleeve. No hidden dagger detected, which Hallowmere's guards found suspicious in itself.

Ashenfold's counter-offer arrived by noon. It would pay the tariff in turnips. Brackwater declined, on the grounds that it could not tell what it was being paid in. Ashenfold then offered the swords back, if somebody would find the wish spell and ask it politely. Nobody has. The cleric who might have, a dwarf named Brenna Tolliver, said only that wishes "don't take returns."

The real fight is at the bridge. Gorvash Pennyfist, who has collected tolls on Quillmarch Bridge for nine winters, announced that his toll of three copper applies to "anything that rolls, walks, or sprouts." The turnips are carried, which he says is a loophole. Brackwater says the loophole is the whole country.

Count it as the field sees it. Two tariffs, one toll, 212 turnips, and no weapon in the whole parley. Every soldier in both baronies has gone home to supper. A farmer's wife near the crossing told me the turnips make a decent stew and nobody has asked her for a duty on that. I took the stew. Field rations are the only honest part of this war.

Tension stands at four siege-days, up from zero at the last report. Nobody is armed. Everybody is angry. That is how you know the peace is working.

Ironjaw, filed from the front.
